concepts.label: Development, inequality & sustainable livelihoods
concepts.concept: Examines how inequality, institutions and environmental change shape livelihoods through sociology, economics, policy analysis, colonial and Indigenous histories, farming and mixed research methods.

concepts.label: Development economics & public policy
concepts.concept: Prioritises economic explanations of distribution and policy: microeconomics, macroeconomics, public and behavioural economics, econometrics and mathematical methods, applied alongside farming, environmental governance and qualitative inquiry.

concepts.label: Development sociology, culture & communication
concepts.concept: Investigates power and social change through sociology, colonial and Indigenous histories, environmental justice, African heritage, media and public communication, supported by qualitative research and statistical foundations.

targetSubstance: The broad response now gives sustained sociology, inequality and political-economic analysis, actual farming/environmental governance, colonial/Indigenous land-food history and mixed methods. It responds materially to development substance rather than generic law/governance alone. Specialist agrarian/rural-household theories and integrated development fieldwork remain limits, not reasons for an unsupported no-match.

courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.contribution: Mandatory Year-1 PPD.

evidenceFields.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

evidenceFields.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courses.name: Introduction to Economics
courses.contribution: Direct economic foundation in markets, allocation and macroeconomic processes for studying distribution and policy.

evidenceFields.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
evidenceFields.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
evidenceFields.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

courses.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
courses.contribution: Direct comparative analysis of institutions, democracy and political outcomes supports explanations of unequal governance and development.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.

courses.name: Introduction to Sociology
courses.contribution: Direct social explanation of stratification, class, race and gender using classical and decolonial sociology.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courses.contribution: Direct research foundation: empirical questions, design, surveys, statistical analysis and R support investigation of inequality and development claims.

evidenceFields.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.

courses.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
courses.contribution: Direct study of environmental justice, social movements, decolonial approaches and degrowth connects inequality and environmental change.

evidenceFields.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

courses.name: Theory of International Relations
courses.contribution: Direct international-relations theories, North–South relations, colonial legacies and global environmental cooperation support multi-level institutional analysis.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.

courses.name: Media & the Environment
courses.contribution: Direct analysis of environmental representation, Indigenous/postcolonial media, risk and public debate connects communication with environmental-development questions.

evidenceFields.description2: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.

Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.

courses.name: Modern Sociology
courses.contribution: Direct contemporary social theory for power, modernity, colonial relations, stigma and intersecting inequalities.

evidenceFields.description2: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.

courses.name: Law, Society & Justice
courses.contribution: Direct socio-legal analysis of law, social change, justice, race and gender; also provides the formal foundation for public international law where selected.

evidenceFields.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. courses.contribution: Direct historical investigation of modern global change, colonialism, decolonisation and globalisation supports interpretation of present inequalities.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. courses.name: Climate Change
courses.contribution: Direct analysis of climate impacts, agriculture, justice and governance, including stakeholder inquiry, links environmental change to social consequences.

evidenceFields.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. courses.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
courses.contribution: Direct microeconomic analysis of choices, incentives, market outcomes and externalities supports explanation of distribution and economic policy.

evidenceFields.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.

courses.name: Public Economics
courses.contribution: Direct public-policy economics of public goods, externalities, taxation, redistribution, welfare and efficiency supports analysis of inequality and intervention.

evidenceFields.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.

courses.name: Native American Histories
courses.contribution: Direct Indigenous histories of dispossession, colonial power, food sovereignty and ecological knowledge connect development justice to land and livelihoods; reciprocal collaboration informs research ethics.

evidenceFields.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.

evidenceFields.description2: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. courses.name: Econometrics
courses.contribution: Direct quantitative investigation through regression, OLS/GLS, instrumental variables and inference; supports testing economic explanations with data.

evidenceFields.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

courses.name: Public Policy Analysis
courses.contribution: Direct public-policy analysis in globalisation, using sugar and national/international policy arenas; policy memos connect institutions and food-related decisions.

evidenceFields.description2: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.

courses.name: Governance of Sustainability
courses.contribution: Direct institutional and stakeholder analysis of food, water, energy and climate governance; applied policy advice/evaluation addresses power, participation and sustainability.

evidenceFields.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
evidenceFields.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.

courses.name: Linear Algebra
courses.contribution: Complementary matrices, least squares and linear-algebra methods strengthen econometric and quantitative model reasoning.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
evidenceFields.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
evidenceFields.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
evidenceFields.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation

courses.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
courses.contribution: Complementary political philosophy examines legitimacy, justice, welfare and non-European/decolonial perspectives behind economic-policy choices.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
evidenceFields.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
evidenceFields.discipline: Political philosophy; History of political thought
evidenceFields.topics: Society, rights and political authority; Classical political thought; Sovereignty and political realism; Enlightenment and revolution; Liberalism and conservatism; Feminism; Nationalism; Socialism and communism; Empire, race and decolonization; Welfare state and libertarianism; Neoliberalism; Justice
evidenceFields.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction

courses.name: Behavioral Economics
courses.contribution: Direct behavioural economics examines heuristics, biases, framing and experimental approaches to decisions underlying policy responses.

evidenceFields.description2: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

courses.name: Probability & Statistics
courses.contribution: Direct probability, estimation, inference and simulation develop the mathematical basis for interpreting quantitative economic evidence.

evidenceFields.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
evidenceFields.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
evidenceFields.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
evidenceFields.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

courses.name: European Union Politics
courses.contribution: Complementary study of European integration, supranational institutions and policy gives a concrete regional case of international economic governance.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
evidenceFields.discipline: European Union politics; Political science; Public policy
evidenceFields.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
evidenceFields.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis

courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courses.contribution: Direct rhetorical analysis, speeches, debate and storytelling prepare critical and effective public communication about contested social issues.

evidenceFields.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
evidenceFields.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
evidenceFields.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
evidenceFields.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

courses.name: Histories of Gender
courses.contribution: Direct historical inquiry into gender, slavery, health, confinement and activism supports analysis of intersecting power relations; its North American focus is bounded.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
evidenceFields.discipline: History; Gender studies; Queer studies; Carceral studies
evidenceFields.topics: Gender and intersectionality; Body sovereignty; Heteronormativity and compulsory heterosexuality; Homonationalism; Rainbow capitalism; Masculinity and sexuality; Queer ageing and memory; Slavery and racialized gender histories; Family and socialization; Health and pathologization; Media bias and book bans; Incarceration; Queer activism and resistance
evidenceFields.methods: Historical primary-source research; Intersectional analysis; Oral-history interviewing; Critical interpretation of memoir and cultural representations; Arts-based research; Community-engaged activist art; Reflective analysis

courses.name: Ethics
courses.contribution: Complementary ethical argument, including care ethics, supports evaluation of responsibilities and fairness in social-development inquiry.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
evidenceFields.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
evidenceFields.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

courses.name: Introduction to Film & Media
courses.contribution: Complementary film/media foundations and feminist/postcolonial interpretation prepare critical analysis of how social groups and development issues are represented.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.
evidenceFields.topics: Film form and meaning; Cinematography, editing and sound; Mise-en-scène, narrative and performance; Early cinema; German Expressionism and Soviet montage; Classical Hollywood and European New Waves; Feminist film theory; Postcolonial media; Blockbusters; Television and digital platforms; Representation and spectatorship; Media convergence
evidenceFields.methods: Close film and media analysis; Historical and cultural contextualization; Application of feminist and postcolonial film theory; Independent analytical or creative-analytical media research

courses.name: African Art & Heritage
courses.contribution: Complementary West African heritage study analyses social meaning, authority, colonial dispossession and restitution; gives a specific cultural-power case rather than general development anthropology.

evidenceFields.description2: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
evidenceFields.profile: Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings. Students study sculpture, masks and other forms across regional contexts before tracing African art's role in European modernism, the Harlem Renaissance and African artistic renewal. Colonial dispossession, museum collecting and restitution form a major later strand. An independent paper develops a research question supported by scholarly evidence.
evidenceFields.discipline: African art history; Cultural heritage studies; Museum studies
evidenceFields.topics: Western African artistic traditions; Sculpture, masks and visual languages; Art, religion and social authority; Regional traditions in Nigeria, the Niger region, Atlantic forests and Congo; African influences on European modernism; Harlem Renaissance and diaspora; Art Nègre and the Ecole de Dakar; Colonial looting; Universal museums; Museum acquisition and display; Restitution and repatriation
evidenceFields.methods: Visual and contextual art-historical analysis; Comparative interpretation of artistic traditions; Analysis of primary artistic and critical texts; Heritage-restitution case analysis; Scholarly literature review and annotated bibliography; Independent art-historical research

courses.name: Media & Race
courses.contribution: Direct analysis of media and racial power through archive, participant observation and PhotoVoice/podcast methods supports critical social inquiry and representation.

evidenceFields.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.

evidenceFields.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

courses.name: Persuasive Communication
courses.contribution: Direct framing and persuasion applied through sustainability/community projects link communication to social and environmental action.

evidenceFields.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
evidenceFields.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
evidenceFields.discipline: Communication studies; Social psychology; Applied ethics
evidenceFields.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
evidenceFields.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

courses.name: The Documentary
courses.contribution: Direct documentary research, interviewing and ethical representation develop public communication grounded in evidence; no compulsory international placement is claimed.

evidenceFields.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
evidenceFields.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.

evidenceFields.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice
